body:
Why international principles are necessary

Space activities cross national boundaries in ways that ordinary activities on land generally do not. A satellite launched by one country may pass over many others, and fragments from a damaged spacecraft can threaten users from several nations.

International principles therefore seek to permit exploration while promoting peaceful cooperation, responsible conduct and the protection of other users' interests.

The principal foundational agreement is the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, formally titled the Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies.

Important provisions of the Outer Space Treaty

ArticleCentral principle
IOuter space is free for exploration and use by all states, for the benefit and in the interests of all countries.
IIOuter space and celestial bodies cannot be appropriated by a state through a claim of sovereignty, occupation or another means.
IIISpace activities must accord with international law, including the United Nations Charter, with regard to peace and security.
IVNuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction may not be placed in Earth orbit or stationed in outer space. The Moon and other celestial bodies must be used exclusively for peaceful purposes.
VIStates bear international responsibility for national space activities, including those conducted by private entities.
VIILaunching states are internationally liable for damage caused by their space objects and component parts.
VIIIThe state of registry retains jurisdiction and control over registered space objects; ownership is not lost merely because an object is in space.
IXStates must show due regard for other states' interests and address potentially harmful interference through appropriate consultation.

Peaceful use does not mean that every military connection is prohibited

Article IV contains specific restrictions. It prohibits placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in Earth orbit, installing such weapons on celestial bodies or stationing them elsewhere in space.

The Moon and other celestial bodies are reserved exclusively for peaceful purposes. Military bases, weapons testing and military manoeuvres on those bodies are prohibited. However, the treaty expressly permits military personnel to participate in scientific research or other peaceful activities.

Thus, the treaty should not be read as imposing a blanket prohibition on every satellite with a military connection. Its actual restrictions and the location to which they apply must be distinguished carefully.

Non-appropriation and satellite ownership

Under Article II, a country cannot declare the Moon or an orbital region to be its national territory merely because it reached or uses that location. This is the principle of non-appropriation.

However, Article VIII distinguishes space itself from objects that humans send into space. A launched satellite can continue to have an owner. The state on whose registry it is recorded retains jurisdiction and control over the space object, subject to the treaty.

Do not confuse territory with property. A state cannot claim sovereignty over the Moon, but the treaty does not abolish ownership of a human-made satellite operating in space.

Why private companies remain connected to state responsibility

Article VI establishes that a state bears international responsibility for its national activities in outer space, whether government agencies or non-governmental entities carry them out.

Activities by non-governmental entities require authorisation and continuing supervision by the appropriate state. Consequently, permitting a private company to design, launch or operate a spacecraft does not remove the relevant state's treaty responsibilities.

This principle explains why governments remain involved in the oversight of private space activities even after opening the sector to commercial participation.

Prelims focus

  • The Outer Space Treaty dates from 1967.
  • Article I concerns freedom of exploration and use for the benefit of all countries.
  • Article II prohibits national appropriation of outer space and celestial bodies.
  • Article IV restricts weapons of mass destruction in space and requires peaceful use of celestial bodies.
  • Article VI covers state responsibility for governmental and non-governmental space activities.
  • Trap: The ban on national appropriation does not mean that ownership of artificial satellites is prohibited.

[Sources: Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies, 1967, Articles I–IV and VI–IX, treaty text reproduced in NASA History, Outer Space Treaty – 1967, accessed 4 November 2026; United Nations General Assembly, Resolution 2222 (XXI), annex containing the Outer Space Treaty.]

pictures.alt: The treaty prohibits specified weapons and military activities but permits peaceful exploration and peaceful work by military personnel.
pictures.caption: The treaty specifies prohibited activities but permits peaceful scientific use of space.

title: The Outer Space Treaty: Peaceful Use, Non-Appropriation and State Responsibility

body:
Responsibility and liability are related but different

International responsibility concerns a state's duty to ensure that its national space activities conform to the applicable international rules. Under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, this duty extends to activities carried out by private entities.

International liability concerns the legal obligation arising when a space object causes damage for which a launching state is liable. Article VII of the Outer Space Treaty establishes a foundational liability principle.

The Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, 1972, usually called the Liability Convention, develops this principle further.

Who is a launching state?

For the basic liability framework, a launching state includes a state that launches or procures the launch of a space object, or a state from whose territory or facility the object is launched. More than 1 state may qualify in connection with a particular launch.

The important prelims distinction is that a private company owning or operating a satellite does not make the international launching-state framework disappear.

Where the damage occurs determines the basic liability rule

Damage on Earth's surface or to an aircraft in flight

Under the Liability Convention, a launching state is absolutely liable for damage caused by its space object on the surface of Earth or to an aircraft in flight. As a basic rule, the injured party need not establish fault by the launching state to invoke this form of liability.

For example, if a component of a launched space object falls to the ground and damages a building, the basic applicable rule is absolute liability. The convention contains further qualifications and procedures, but they are not needed to identify the central distinction.

Damage to another space object in outer space

When a space object causes damage to another space object, or to persons or property aboard it, in outer space, the convention generally uses fault-based liability. Liability in this situation depends on fault attributable to the relevant launching state or persons for whom it is responsible.

For example, if 2 satellites collide in orbit, the basic rule is not automatically the same as that governing a fragment that damages property on the ground.

Location is the key distinction: Damage on Earth's surface or to aircraft in flight is associated with absolute liability. Damage to another space object in outer space is generally associated with fault-based liability.

International institutions and cooperation

The United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) provides an international forum for discussing the peaceful uses of outer space and the development of related principles. It became a permanent committee in 1959.

The United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA) supports international cooperation and serves as the secretariat for COPUOS and its subcommittees. Neither COPUOS nor UNOOSA acts as a universal licensing office for individual private satellite launches.

Voluntary sustainability guidelines

In June 2019, COPUOS adopted the preamble and 21 Guidelines for the Long-term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities. The United Nations General Assembly welcomed their adoption in December 2019.

The guidelines address matters such as the safe conduct of space operations, cooperation, information exchange and the reduction of risks to the orbital environment. They encourage states and relevant organisations to improve their practices.

These guidelines are voluntary and non-legally binding. Their status differs from treaty obligations undertaken by states that are parties to an applicable treaty.

Prelims focus

  • The Outer Space Treaty dates from 1967; its Articles VI and VII address responsibility and liability.
  • The Liability Convention dates from 1972.
  • Surface damage and aircraft damage are associated with absolute liability.
  • Damage to another space object in outer space is generally governed by fault-based liability.
  • COPUOS became a permanent United Nations committee in 1959.
  • Trap: The 21 COPUOS sustainability guidelines adopted in 2019 are voluntary, not a new binding treaty.

[Sources: Outer Space Treaty, 1967, Articles VI–VII, treaty text reproduced in NASA History, Outer Space Treaty – 1967, accessed 4 November 2026; United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, Liability Convention, introduction and summary of liability rules, accessed 4 November 2026; United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, institutional background; United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, Guidelines for the Long-term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities, Adoption and background, June and December 2019, accessed 4 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Launching states face absolute liability for surface or aircraft damage, and generally fault-based liability for damage to another space object in outer space.
pictures.caption: Absolute liability applies to surface and aircraft damage; fault-based liability generally applies to space-object damage in outer space.

pictures.alt: Timeline from permanent COPUOS in 1959 through binding treaties in 1967 and 1972 to voluntary sustainability guidelines adopted and welcomed in 2019.
pictures.caption: International space governance developed through treaties and later sustainability guidance.

title: Liability for Space Damage and International Cooperation

body:
Why India's space-sector structure has changed

India's space programme was developed principally through public institutions, especially the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). As satellite technology and its applications expanded, private organisations also gained opportunities to design spacecraft, develop launch systems, provide satellite services and participate in manufacturing.

India announced major space-sector reforms in 2020 to expand participation by non-governmental entities. The Indian Space Policy 2023 further clarified the different roles of public institutions and private participants.

The central idea is cooperation with distinct responsibilities. Public institutions continue to develop strategic and advanced capabilities, while private entities can carry out a wider range of operational and commercial activities under the applicable national framework.

Four public institutions with different roles

InstitutionFull nameMain role
DOSDepartment of SpaceOversees and coordinates the implementation of India's space policy and national space programme.
ISROIndian Space Research OrganisationDevelops space technologies, undertakes research and advanced missions, and supports the national space programme.
IN-SPACeIndian National Space Promotion and Authorisation CentrePromotes, enables and authorises space activities, and facilitates appropriate participation by non-governmental entities.
NSILNewSpace India LimitedGovernment-owned commercial enterprise supporting commercial space activities, technology transfer and industry participation.

Department of Space

DOS provides the overarching governmental framework for India's space activities. Its role differs from directly manufacturing a satellite or selling a commercial launch service.

Indian Space Research Organisation

ISRO is India's national space agency. Its work includes space research, development of advanced technologies, scientific and exploratory missions, and the creation of capabilities needed for national priorities. Its expertise and facilities can also support wider industry participation under the applicable arrangements.

Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre

IN-SPACe is an autonomous government organisation under DOS. It acts as a single-window agency for promoting and authorising space activities, including those undertaken by non-governmental entities.

It helps private participants enter the sector, facilitates access to relevant space infrastructure and expertise, and performs authorisation and oversight functions. The distinction is important: its principal role is not to replace ISRO as the country's research and development agency or NSIL as a commercial enterprise.

NewSpace India Limited

NSIL is a government-owned commercial enterprise established in 2019. Its activities include commercialising space technologies and services, supporting technology transfer and encouraging industrial participation in the production and delivery of space systems.

NSIL and IN-SPACe should not be treated as interchangeable. One has a commercial and industry-development role; the other has promotion, enablement and authorisation responsibilities.

What private entities may do

Under the policy framework, non-governmental entities may participate in activities such as developing satellites and launch vehicles, operating space-based services, providing ground infrastructure and contributing to space-safety capabilities, subject to the applicable authorisation and oversight requirements.

Private participation can also include manufacturing components, producing satellite applications and processing Earth-observation data for users.

Example: a private Earth-observation satellite

Consider an Indian company that wants to operate a satellite to provide information about crops and water availability. The company may design the spacecraft and develop its services. IN-SPACe is relevant to the authorisation and enablement of the proposed activity. ISRO's technological expertise or facilities may be relevant where an appropriate arrangement exists. NSIL may participate through commercial space services, but using NSIL is not necessarily a required step for every private satellite mission.

Once the satellite operates, the need for safe conduct, collision-risk management and eventual disposal remains. Private ownership does not cancel the international responsibility of the appropriate state under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty.

Private participation is not the same as privatisation of ISRO. The Indian Space Policy 2023 assigns complementary roles to ISRO, IN-SPACe, NSIL, DOS and non-governmental entities.

Prelims focus

  • Major reforms expanding private participation were announced in 2020.
  • Indian Space Policy 2023 clarifies institutional responsibilities.
  • ISRO focuses on research, technology development and national space missions.
  • IN-SPACe promotes and authorises space activities and enables private participation.
  • NSIL is a government-owned commercial space enterprise established in 2019.
  • Trap: IN-SPACe is not the same institution as NSIL, and expanding private participation does not mean ISRO has been privatised.

[Sources: Government of India, Indian Space Policy 2023, section 3: Strategy, section 4: Non-Governmental Entities, section 5: IN-SPACe, and sections 6–8: ISRO, NSIL and DOS, printed pp. 5–10, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, Roles and Responsibilities of IN-SPACe, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, Space Reforms, sections on IN-SPACe and NSIL, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, Clarification Regarding Media Reports, 6 September 2026, on the continuing roles of public institutions and private-sector reforms.]

pictures.alt: Three technicians in protective clothing carefully assemble a small satellite in a contemporary Indian space company cleanroom.
pictures.caption: Private companies can develop spacecraft and services within India's national space framework.

pictures.alt: IN-SPACe authorises private satellite activities; ISRO and NSIL offer possible support under DOS policy coordination and state responsibility.
pictures.caption: Private satellite operations involve distinct authorisation, technology and commercial functions.

title: India's Space Sector: Public Institutions and Private Participation
